title: Guru Nanak: wonder
hook: the first Guru's light: wonder at the one Creator in all
tomorrow: how does a disciple become the Guru? not how you'd guess.

segments.voice: Yesterday, your Ardas: remember first, then ask, then the good of all. Tonight Simran is out back, flat on the trampoline.

Half the people on a beach at sunset are filming it, and the sunset never quite fits on the screen. Simran and Maya are on the backyard trampoline after dark, phones face down for once, because Maya leaves for a different college in the fall and they're counting nights. Maya points up. At her cousin's wedding, she says, people waved little lamps on a tray. Do Sikhs do that? Simran knows this one, sort of. When the first Guru looked up, he saw a tray of lamps already lit. The sky was the platter.
screen: `THE SUNSET WON'T FIT ON THE SCREEN.` → `A TRAY OF LITTLE LAMPS.` → `THE SKY WAS THE PLATTER.`

segments.voice: Tradition tells it this way. Guru Nanak came to the temple at Puri at evening worship, when lamps were waved on a platter, and he didn't join in. He sang the hymn now on Ang 13. In paraphrase: the sky is the platter, the sun and moon are the lamps, the stars are the pearls; the scented wind is the incense, the forests are flowers. All creation is already doing the aarti. The feeling in it has a name: vismaad, wonder. In Asa di Var he lists it: wonder at the sound, wonder at the knowledge, wonder at the creatures, wonder at their colors. Now the debate, because Sikhs still sing this hymn, and not all the same way. At some historic gurdwaras, lamps are waved while it's sung. Their best case: it's old custom at those seats, and the hymn about the sky is still its heart; the hands help the eyes look up. Elsewhere, following the Sikh code, it's sung with no lamps at all. Their best case: the Guru looked away from the small tray to the big one; singing it is the aarti. Neither side stops singing it. Here's one for a friend tonight: Guru Nanak's aarti has no lamp but the sun and the moon. Maya is quiet a while. So wonder is the whole point, she says. Simran says: the starting point.
screen: `PURI, AT EVENING WORSHIP.` · `SUN AND MOON ARE THE LAMPS.` · `VISMAAD: WONDER.` · `LAMPS, OR NO LAMPS?` · then, large: `WONDER.`

segments.voice: Go to a window or step outside and look up for the whole sit. Find the biggest light you can see, then the smallest; in daylight, follow one cloud. Don't name anything and don't photograph it. Just let it be bigger than you for a while.
Guru Nanak: the first Guru, whose light is wonder. He looked past the tray of lamps to the sky, and sang that it was already worshipping.
For the road: wonder, the whole sky as the platter, already lit. The first of ten lights.

howItsDone: Sikhs sing Guru Nanak's aarti hymn, 'gagan mai thaal', as part of Kirtan Sohila, the prayer before sleep, and in gurdwaras in the evening; at some historic gurdwaras lamps are waved during it, while elsewhere it is sung without lamps.

chat.says: maya asked if sikhs wave lamps at prayers like at her cousin's wedding. what do i tell her
options: tell her Guru Nanak sang that the sky's the platter; some places add lamps, some don't.
tell her no; Guru Nanak banned lamps, so a gurdwara with one breaks the rules.
tell her yes; every gurdwara waves lamps at night, same as at the wedding.
chat.meaning: On Ang 13 Guru Nanak sings the sky as the aarti platter. Some historic gurdwaras wave lamps with it; others sing it with none.

aarti.meaning: worship with lamps on a platter; also Guru Nanak's hymn

Asa di Var.meaning: a long hymn of Guru Nanak's in the Guru Granth Sahib

Puri.meaning: a temple city in eastern India, in the story
